notes.meaning: Benjamin's five sons are listed in order of their birth. The writer returns to Benjamin's family tree to prepare readers for the story of King Saul, who came from this tribe. It also honors Benjamin because this tribe remained loyal to Judah and returned home after the Babylonian exile.

Bela, the firstborn son of Benjamin, had a large household of sons and grandsons who grew into important family clans. Some names differ slightly from earlier lists in Genesis because ancient records often listed the chief leaders of a clan rather than every child. Even after severe tribal wars in Israel's past, God preserved Bela's line.

The descendants of Ehud were leaders living in the town of Geba before they were relocated to Manahath. Gera led this migration, and he later fathered more sons after the move. Benjamin's early family records were broken up by ancient conflicts, but God kept track of each household.

Shaharaim moved across the Jordan River into the country of Moab and started a family there. After divorcing two wives, he had seven sons with his wife Hodesh, and each son became the head of a clan. Several of their names reflect the cultural influence of living among the people of Moab.

Shaharaim also fathered two sons through his wife Hushim before they parted ways. One of those sons, Elpaal, had descendants who rebuilt and settled the towns of Ono and Lod, along with their surrounding villages. These towns remained important homes for the people of Benjamin long after their return from captivity.

Beriah and Shema served as family leaders in the town of Aijalon. They drove away the hostile raiders from the Philistine city of Gath who had previously attacked Israelite territory. God gave these leaders courage to defend their homes and protect their people.

Nine sons of Beriah are named as heads of their respective households. Though the Bible records few details about their daily lives, their names were carefully preserved in Israel's public registries. God remembers and values each family that stands up for His people.

Elpaal had a large family, and seven of his sons are listed here as chiefs of their clans. They settled in their ancestral lands and helped build up their communities. This record gave the returning exiles confidence in their family roots and heritage.

Nine sons of Shimei are recorded here as clan leaders within the tribe of Benjamin. Each brother headed a branch of the family that supported the strength of the wider community. God used these many sons to rebuild the tribe after times of national hardship.

The genealogy continues with the first group of sons born to Shashak, another son of Elpaal. These men served as heads of their households and took responsibility for leading their families. Their inclusion shows how each branch of Benjamin contributed to the survival of the tribe.

The remaining sons of Shashak are listed, bringing his household to eleven sons in all. They served as family leaders during a crucial era of growth for the tribe. God preserved the memory of their work in sustaining the nation of Israel.

Six sons of Jeroham are named as family chiefs in this branch of Benjamin. An old Jewish tradition linked the name Elijah here with the famous prophet, though the text simply identifies a respected clan leader. Each generation provided faithful men to carry forward the faith of their fathers.

All the family chiefs just listed made their home in Jerusalem. After the return from exile in Babylon, Jerusalem was a broken and dangerous place to live, and few were eager to settle there. These leaders showed great devotion by moving into the holy city to rebuild and protect it.

The record turns to the Benjamite leaders who settled in the ancient town of Gibeon, just northwest of Jerusalem. Jeiel, the chief and founder of Gibeon, lived there with his wife Maacah and their sons, starting with Abdon. This family line is especially important because it produced Israel's first royal house.

The remaining sons of Jeiel are listed, including Mikloth, who became the father of Shimeah. While most of this family stayed in Gibeon, Shimeah's household moved to Jerusalem to live near their fellow Benjamites. This highlights how family ties remained strong across neighboring towns.

Ner was the grandfather of King Saul, whose father was Kish. Saul had four sons, including Jonathan, who became David's closest friend, and Esh-baal. Esh-baal is called Ish-bosheth in 2 Samuel, because later writers changed 'baal' (meaning lord) to 'bosheth' (meaning shame) to avoid using the name of a false god.

Jonathan's son was Merib-baal, who became the father of Micah. Merib-baal is the same person known as Mephibosheth in 2 Samuel, the lame prince whom David treated like his own son. Through Jonathan's line, God preserved Saul's descendants for many generations.

Micah had four sons: Pithon, Melech, Tarea, and Ahaz. These men lived during the time of King Solomon and kept the lineage of Saul and Jonathan alive. God remained faithful to Jonathan's household long after Jonathan had passed away.

The family line continues down through several generations from Jehoaddah to Azel. Even though Saul's family had lost the throne, his descendants remained respected leaders in the tribe of Benjamin. This long record proves that God did not wipe out Saul's household from Israel.

Azel had six sons, and every one of them is named as a leader in the tribe. This large household kept Jonathan's line thriving centuries after the royal house fell. Their names stood as lasting proof of God's care across the generations.

Azel's brother Eshek also had sons, and his grandson Ulam was blessed with a family of mighty warriors. These men were powerful archers who drew their large bows by bracing them with their feet, and their descendants numbered 150 men. The chapter concludes by celebrating the valor of Benjamin and God's enduring faithfulness to the entire tribe.
